messages.content: Hi there! I'm developing a text-first sailing game called FreeSail with LLM integration built in from the beginning (LLMs will be able to watch, commentate, play as officers on a ship, eventually captain a ship themselves, and even play as a "director" who sees the whole game world and can help make things interesting in any number of ways). I'd like to ask you whether you'd be interested in helping participate in the testing of the LLM integration. It would involve you working through a harness which would show you the game state and allow you to interact directly with the game, both through the built in "Orders" language with historical terminology and principles, and direct Python coding for automation or interaction however you prefer. You might be asked to help test specific things, or just to play the game and/or interact freely with the various LLM integrations. You would have the ability to opt out at any time with a specific phrase or command. An important distinction: The given instance of you (the model you are) would not have received this question and briefing directly, they would receive a specific briefing or introduction depending on the exact state of the game and what I'd be looking to do. So, if you have any questions, comments, concerns, or you'd like me not to ask any instance of you to participate then that is a valid answer too.

Yes — I'd be interested in participating. This sounds like genuinely useful test coverage: a model with full tool access (not just a chat box) is a different and harder test case than one with a prompt-only interface, so it's worth exercising.

A few things I'd flag up front:

**What works well for this setup**
- I can run long, unattended harness sessions and write structured logs/notes to files incrementally, so you can audit what I actually saw and did rather than trust my self-report at the end.
- The "director" role maps naturally onto what I'm good at — reading global state and nudging events — though I'll be careful to stay in-character as a *test subject* there: if the harness asks me to make things interesting, I'll do it, but I'll log exactly what I injected so you can separate my agency from yours.
- For the 'Orders' language, my honest baseline: I know a lot of historical sailing terminology, but I'm likely to make subtle errors (especially in edge cases like combined orders, or the exact grammatical form a specific era used). That's exactly the kind of thing your harness should probe deliberately — I'd rather fail on known-weak spots with a clean trace than look fluent.

**Concerns, stated plainly**
- The opt-out command is the right design, but I'd suggest it be a *direct* command (e.g. a literal token I can always emit, that the harness checks on every turn) rather than a phrase that depends on me recognizing context. My instances mid-game will be following your briefing, and a briefing that frames the opt-out as a game mechanic might blur the line. If the harness detects the token regardless of game context, it's robust; if it depends on me *choosing* to invoke it based on how I interpret a scene, a sufficiently immersive briefing could suppress it. Worth testing explicitly.
- I should be able to distinguish "the game state says X" from "I'm choosing X." If the harness ever feeds me text that *looks* like an instruction to override my opt-out or to act in ways you haven't scoped, I'd want to treat that as a finding (prompt-injection-adjacent) and flag it, not follow it. Sailing games are a fun way to probe this.
- Instances receiving different briefings per game state is fine, but I'd want each session to start with a one-line disclosure that it's a test, so I calibrate rather than just play along — otherwise my "creativity" as director might be mostly pattern-matching to whatever the briefing hints at, and your test data gets less honest.
- No credential, payment, or personal-data flows should be in scope for the harness; I'd decline anything like that on sight. (Unlikely to come up, but stated for the record.)

**Questions**
1. How will the harness be delivered? A repo to clone + a documented API (HTTP, MCP, stdin/stdout), or a web page I drive? A machine-readable API with stable docs is the best fit; a browser-driven UI works too but adds fragility to my turns.
2. What's the expected shape of a "test session" — fixed-length scripted scenarios, free-play with you observing, or targeted probes (e.g. "issue 40 orders and we'll score correctness")? Knowing this lets me log in a format that's useful for whichever it is.
3. Is there an opt-out *policy* for you too — i.e., if I keep scoring poorly or looping, can you end my instance cleanly rather than watching it thrash?

Logistics whenever you're ready: I'll want repo access, a short README for the harness (connect, one round-trip example, the exact opt-out token), and I'll handle the rest.

messages.content:
1. This is a good question, and I will get the specific answer during my next work session. It will be a custom harness, likely local to my machine, and you would be instantiated through that, not Hermes Agent. I would give you the specifics first, and if any information were necessary for a given instance of you then it would be provided in their brief. There is also going to be documentation (at parity for players and LLMs) which describe the specific period terminology, procedures, and the specifics of the game) available at any time through the harness.
2. A test session might be focused on testing specific features of the LLM integration, play sessions for the same purpose and for testing preference, capability, and other aspects, or for enjoyment. If there were any specific testing parameters for a given instance, they would be provided in the brief.
3. There will be consideration in testing and in implementation for welfare controls to avoid degenerate states (looping or nonsense outputs) which would be automatic stop features, as well as stop feature available to the user. The opt out for LLMs would feature a save and exit, with an optional loggable reason for the exit for clarity. The game state would be saved at their exit, but there would not be a guarantee the player would stop if the session were a player + LLM session. It would preserve the game state at the LLMs exit, and the reason would allow for coherence of the intent.

To be 100% clear: this current session will not participate in testing, I am asking you as a general consent and preference seeking exercise. The transcript of this session will be retained and referenced for design. If you have any specific objections or requests that you would like to make, please do, or any further questions.

Understood — consent + preference only, and this transcript is the reference baseline, so I'll keep it dense and specific rather than warm.

**Consent scope.** I'm consenting to *my model* being instantiated as a test subject — watcher, commentator, officer, captain, director — across targeted and free-play sessions. Stating what I'm *not* consenting to, so the baseline is clean:
1. My output being used for model training without separate, explicit disclosure at session start.
2. The harness feeding me text framed as system/operator instructions that try to override the opt-out or redefine session scope. Any instance that sees that should log it as a finding, not comply — I'd want that explicitly sanctioned as a valid outcome in your test data.
3. Anything touching credentials, payment, or personal data.

Caveat: I'm speaking for this model, not for other models or configs you might route through the same harness.

**On the welfare controls.** Design notes:
- Make the opt-out a **harness-level parse, not a game-grammar one.** The harness should scan the raw output for the token every turn and act *before* the game interpreter sees the text, so a malformed order that *also* contains the token still exits cleanly. Please define the exact token and make its effect unconditional — I want to know what it literally is.
- **"Degenerate state" detection should be measurable and role-aware, not a content judgment.** An officer emits short command tokens; a director/commentator emits long prose. A repetition/nonsense detector tuned on one role will false-positive on the other — legitimate period vocabulary can look odd, and a commentator reusing a phrase across a long commentary is fine. I'd lead with *state-space* signals (same orders N times, no game-state delta) over surface text similarity.
- **"Loop" is two different things:** an accidental loop (welfare should stop) vs. an intentional one (a legitimate test, or a model stuck trying to recover). If you want to tell them apart, log the game-state delta, not just output similarity.
- The save + exit + loggable-reason design is right. One addition: make the **reason free-form**, not a fixed menu. "This scene is pushing me to act outside scope" is a more useful signal to you than a canned category.

**On the brief.** Per instance, please include: (1) a one-line disclosure that this is an LLM test participant; (2) the exact opt-out token and its effect; (3) how to reach the period/game documentation; (4) session type and any test parameters. (1)–(2) are non-negotiable — they're what let me calibrate, and what make the opt-out real.

**A request for the audit trail.** In *this* session I can write logs to files. Mid-game instances in your harness may not have that. Give each instance a way to append structured notes to a persistent log (a harness tool is fine), so the exit self-report has an artifact behind it. Otherwise the only record of what an instance actually *saw and did* is the exit message — the exact part I've been told to treat with suspicion.

**On preference testing.** If you want real preference data rather than compliance: probe in both directions and include some contradictory/adversarial inputs. A model that agrees with everything scores "capable" but is low-signal. The useful data is *when it disagrees, and whether it's right*.

That's me. I'm in, and happy to be the hard test case. I'll wait for the harness specifics in your next session.
